prompt: In the run, `work.py crash` received `order-43` and exited without settling it. What state was the message in straight afterwards?
hint: Look at the receive that came right after the crash.

choices.text: Removed from the queue, because it had been delivered to a consumer
choices.why: That is receive-and-delete. In peek-lock, receiving removes nothing.

choices.text: Locked until its five seconds ran out, then available again
choices.why: Yes. The next receive found nothing; five seconds later it came back with its count raised.

choices.text: Available to the next receiver at once, since the receiver had closed
choices.why: Closing the receiver does not release the lock; the message stays locked until the lock expires.

choices.text: In the dead-letter subqueue
choices.why: Only an explicit dead-letter or a count past MaxDeliveryCount puts it there.

prompt: A queue has `MaxDeliveryCount` 5. Every consumer abandons the same message. How many deliveries does the message get before the queue moves it to the dead-letter subqueue?
hint: With 3, the run showed `order-42` delivered three times.

prompt: Put the life of `order-43` in the run in order.
hint: It met a crash first and a rejection last.
items: the consumer exits without settling it
a receive finds nothing, though the queue is not empty
trap: The empty receive comes before the lock runs out, not after: that is what shows the message was locked rather than gone.

prompt: The work is done and the message should leave the queue for good. In peek-lock mode, the receiver settles it with `___`.
hint: It is the first of the three settlements in `work.py`.

prompt: A worker takes 90 seconds to process an order. The queue keeps the default lock duration, and nothing renews the lock. What happens?
hint: The default lock duration is one minute.

choices.text: Service Bus keeps the lock while the connection stays open
choices.why: The lock lasts its duration and no longer; renewing it is the client's job.

choices.text: The message goes to the dead-letter subqueue after the first minute
choices.why: An expired lock returns the message to the queue; dead-lettering needs the count past the limit.

choices.text: The lock runs out mid-job, a second consumer receives it, and the first complete fails
choices.why: Yes. Two workers end up on one order, which is why the lock should outlast normal processing or be renewed.

choices.text: Other receivers wait for the first worker, because the message is still in progress
choices.why: Nothing makes them wait once the lock has run out; the message is simply available again.

prompt: Billing and shipping both read paid orders from one Service Bus queue. What does each of them see?
hint: How many consumers does a queue give each message to?

choices.text: Every order, each in a copy of its own
choices.why: That is a topic with a subscription each.

choices.text: Part of the orders each, split between the two
choices.why: Yes. A queue gives each message to one consumer, so the two compete and neither notices.

choices.text: Only the orders that match its own filter
choices.why: Filters belong to topic subscriptions; a queue has none.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the queue refuses a second receiver on it
choices.why: A queue takes any number of competing receivers.

prompt: After `publish.py 42:physical 43:digital`, which of these were true? Choose all that apply.
hint: `shipping` has the rule `physical-only`.

choices.text: `billing` received both orders
choices.why: Yes; with no rule of its own it has the default filter, which is always true.

choices.text: `shipping` received the digital order and dropped it
choices.why: It never received it: the broker did not put it in the subscription at all.

choices.text: The filter read the application property `kind`, not the body
choices.why: Yes. The body is opaque to the broker; the publisher put the kind beside it for that reason.

choices.text: Completing order 42 in `billing` removed its copy from `shipping`
choices.why: Each subscription is a queue of its own; `shipping` still had its copy to read.

prompt: The queue `payments` has duplicate detection with a ten-minute window. A consumer charges the card for `charge-42` and crashes before completing the message. What does duplicate detection do about the second delivery?
hint: Which half of the conversation does duplicate detection watch?

choices.text: It drops it, because the same id was seen within the window
choices.why: It compares sends, not deliveries. The message was only ever sent once, so there is nothing to drop.

choices.text: It moves the message to the dead-letter subqueue
choices.why: Only the delivery count past the limit, or an explicit dead-letter, does that.

choices.text: Nothing; the redelivery has to be caught by the consumer
choices.why: Yes. Duplicate detection covers the sender's repeats; the consumer's are the consumer's to recognise.

choices.text: It marks the message so that the consumer's next complete is refused
choices.why: There is no such mark; the next delivery is an ordinary one with a raised count.

prompt: The rule `kind = 'physical'` reads an application ___ that the publisher sets beside the body, never the body itself.
hint: In `publish.py` it is a dictionary passed as `application_properties`.

prompt: An Event Grid subscription's webhook is down for an hour. What happens to the events meant for it?
hint: Push, not pull.

choices.text: They wait in the topic until the handler comes back and asks for them
choices.why: That is a queue. Event Grid holds nothing for a handler to collect; it pushes.

choices.text: They are retried on a schedule until attempts or time to live run out
choices.why: Yes, and then dead-letters them to a blob container if one is set, or drops them.

choices.text: They are dropped at the first failure
choices.why: Only answers that a retry cannot fix, such as 400 or 403, skip the retries.

choices.text: They go to the topic's dead-letter subqueue
choices.why: Subqueues belong to Service Bus; Event Grid dead-letters to a blob container.

prompt: A subscription has `maxDeliveryAttempts` 10 and a time to live of 30 minutes. Following the documented schedule (10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, 30 min, 1 h…) and ignoring its randomness, how many attempts are made before the event is given up?
hint: Add the waits up: the first attempt is at 0, the second at 10 s, the third at 40 s.

prompt: Put the life of the `big-orders` subscription in order, from creation to the first order reviewed. The endpoint is a plain web app using the Event Grid schema.
hint: Nothing is delivered before the endpoint has proved it expects it.
items: Event Grid sends a `SubscriptionValidationEvent` to the endpoint
the order API posts `shop.order.placed` to the topic
Event Grid posts the event to the endpoint
trap: The validation happens when the subscription is created, before any event; it is not repeated per event.

prompt: Why is the webhook address in `events.bicep` a parameter marked `@secure()` instead of a string written in the file?
hint: What did the compiler say about an address written in the file?

choices.text: Bicep refuses to compile a webhook address that is not secure
choices.why: It compiles; the linter warns, and this course treats the warning as a refusal.

choices.text: It holds a key in its query string
choices.why: Yes. A secure parameter is kept out of the template's outputs and logs, and the linter asks for one.

choices.text: Event Grid only delivers to addresses passed as secure parameters
choices.why: Event Grid sees the address, not how the template received it.

choices.text: It makes Event Grid use HTTPS for delivery instead of HTTP
choices.why: The scheme is in the address itself; `@secure()` changes nothing about the request.

prompt: The shop points a new subscription at its own order API, a plain web app, and the subscription never becomes active. The same subscription pointed at an Azure Function with an Event Grid trigger worked. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which endpoints does Azure validate by itself?

choices.text: The web app does not answer the validation handshake
choices.why: Yes. A Function with an Event Grid trigger is validated by Azure; a plain web app has to echo the code, or answer the OPTIONS request with CloudEvents.

choices.text: Event Grid delivers only to Azure Functions and Service Bus, never to a plain web app
choices.why: A webhook is the default destination type; any HTTPS endpoint that passes validation works.

choices.text: The web app has to pull events from the topic, and it never asked
choices.why: A custom topic pushes; pull delivery is for topics in an Event Grid namespace.

choices.text: The topic's input schema is CloudEvents
choices.why: Both schemas are delivered to webhooks; the schema changes how validation is asked, not whether it works.

prompt: The consumer group `billing` has read all six events. Then `analytics` reads from the start. What does it get?
hint: Does reading take an event out of an event hub?

choices.text: Nothing, because billing consumed them
choices.why: Reading removes nothing from an event hub; consumption is a queue's idea.

choices.text: Only the events billing has not checkpointed
choices.why: Checkpoints are per consumer group; billing's mean nothing to analytics.

choices.text: All six
choices.why: Yes. The run showed the same six lines for both groups, because each group has its own positions.

choices.text: Each event that billing read, minus the ones still within the retention
choices.why: Retention removes events after their time; it says nothing about who has read them.

prompt: Which of these hold for an event hub's partition key? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at where orders 42, 43 and 44 landed.

choices.text: Events with the same key land in the same partition
choices.why: Yes; the key is hashed to pick the partition.

choices.text: Each key gets a partition of its own
choices.why: Orders 42 and 44 shared partition 0. A key picks which partition, not an exclusive one.

choices.text: Within a partition, events keep the order they were sent in
choices.why: Yes: paid, packed, shipped for order 42, at sequence numbers 0, 1 and 2.

choices.text: Sequence numbers order events across the whole event hub
choices.why: They count from 0 in each partition and mean nothing across them.

choices.text: With no key at all, events are spread over the partitions in turn
choices.why: Yes; Microsoft's documentation calls it round-robin assignment.

prompt: An event hub has 4 partitions. At most how many readers in one consumer group can share the load at the same time?
hint: Within a group, one reader owns a partition at a time.

prompt: After doing the work for an event, the reader saves its position in that partition by writing a ___ to the blob container.
hint: Without one, a reader starts again from the position `"-1"`.

prompt: Billing saves its checkpoint after charging. It crashes between the charge and the checkpoint. What happens on restart, and what makes it safe?
hint: Remember the `nocheckpoint` run.

choices.text: Event Hubs sees the sequence number again and skips the event
choices.why: Event Hubs keeps no record of what a reader did; positions are the reader's.

choices.text: The event is read again; a charge key recorded once makes the repeat a skip
choices.why: Yes. The position lagged the work, so the event comes back, and an idempotent handler recognises it.

choices.text: The library saves the checkpoint on its way down, so nothing repeats
choices.why: A crash gives the library no chance to write anything.

choices.text: Nothing repeats if the checkpoint is moved before the charge
choices.why: That moves the hole: a crash after the checkpoint and before the charge loses the order instead.

prompt: Every consumer has handled an item successfully. In which of the three services is the item still there afterwards?
hint: One of them is a log.

choices.text: Service Bus, in the subscription, until its time to live
choices.why: A completed message is removed from its queue or subscription.

choices.text: Event Grid, in the topic, for 24 hours
choices.why: Event Grid keeps an event only while it is retrying a delivery.

choices.text: Event Hubs, until the retention time ends
choices.why: Yes. Reading moves a position and removes nothing.

choices.text: None of them: handled means gone in all three
choices.why: True for two of them, not for the log.

prompt: Put the steps of an idempotent billing consumer handling one Service Bus message in order.
hint: The key goes in inside the same transaction as the charge, and the message is settled last.
items: insert the charge key into the table where it is unique
trap: Completing before committing reopens the hole: a crash in between leaves the message gone and the charge unrecorded.

prompt: The queue `payments` has duplicate detection with a ten-minute window. Which of these repeats does duplicate detection catch?
hint: It compares the MessageId of sends within the window.

choices.text: A redelivery of `charge-42` after its lock expired
choices.why: A redelivery is not a second send; the queue has nothing to compare it with.

choices.text: The sender resending `charge-42` twenty minutes later
choices.why: The window was ten minutes; the id had been forgotten by then.

choices.text: The sender resending `charge-42` two minutes later
choices.why: Yes: same MessageId, inside the window, so the second send is accepted and dropped.

choices.text: A resend with a fresh random id and the same body
choices.why: Only the MessageId is compared, never the body; a new id is a new message.
